Subject Gateway · The AI Framework Hub

The AI Framework Hub

Whole-school AI literacy from FS2 to Year 13: clear lessons, immersive topic panels, age-appropriate missions, teacher packs and embedded resources.

🤖 The AI Framework Hub
From awareness to systems design
Year Groups

AI Literacy for Every Learner

Choose a year group, open topic panels, launch missions and use linked resources directly inside each pathway.

Discovery

FS2

Notices, sorts, follows instructions and stays safe through play.

Foundation

Year 1

Recognises rules and patterns, gives clear instructions, checks answers and keeps information private.

Foundation

Year 2

Explains how machines learn from examples, builds and tests algorithms, judges answers and protects personal data.

Primary Builder

Year 3

Explains how AI systems are trained, designs and tests a solution, judges reliability and uses data responsibly.

Primary Builder

Year 4

Explains how an AI model learns from data, plans and tests a solution, judges source reliability and uses data responsibly.

Primary Builder

Year 5

Explains how models learn from data, engineers and evaluates a solution, interrogates outputs for bias and applies data rules.

Primary Builder

Year 6

Explains how modern AI systems are built and limited, engineers a solution end to end, challenges outputs with evidence and applies governance.

Secondary Analyst

Year 7

Maps data to model to output, specifies problems, separates supported from unverifiable claims and applies integrity rules.

Secondary Analyst

Year 8

Distinguishes training from deployment, designs decision logic, traces provenance and works within data protection rules.

Secondary Analyst

Year 9

Maps a deployed system end to end, defines safe failure states, audits claims and assigns responsibility.

Senior Systems Designer

Year 10

Analyses how AI systems are engineered, evaluated and governed at scale; designs and defends solutions against criteria.

Senior Systems Designer

Year 11

Evaluates AI systems with independence, documents and defends a substantial solution, and argues evidenced positions on impact.

Senior Systems Designer

Year 12

Critically evaluates AI systems, scopes and delivers an independent project, leads audit and risk assessment, and argues research-informed positions.

Senior Systems Designer

Year 13

Evaluates AI systems and governance at research level, defends a substantial project, leads assurance and produces original analysis.

Missions

AI Challenge Routes

Age-appropriate missions for each year group, with brief, steps and success criteria.

FS2

Play · Notice · Explain

Press, wave, watch and notice what causes a response. Explain what happened and why using pictures, cards or partner talk.

Year 1–2

Rules · Patterns · Safety

Write or say an instruction, let a partner follow it, then improve the unclear part.

Year 3–6

Data · Design · Check

Train and test a simple paper model, name the features and improve a rule that was wrong or unfair.

Year 7–9

Evidence · Bias · Impact

Audit an AI output or workflow. Identify evidence, missing context, bias, impact and one safeguard.

Year 10–13

Risk · Governance · Defence

Decide whether an AI system should be approved, revised or rejected. Define harms, risk register, mitigations and responsibility.

Teacher Portal

Teaching Packs

Topic-linked packs with intent, vocabulary, misconception, lesson sequence, support/stretch, evidence and resources.

FS2 · Cause, Effect and Simple Sensors

Strand: AI Conceptual Understanding

Downloads this teaching pack as a Word-compatible document.

Subject-hub teaching route

Teach the lesson as a clear enquiry: hook image, core knowledge, modelled thinking, guided activity, independent judgement and exit evidence. Students should leave with a visible artefact: annotated prompt, diagram, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement.

Curriculum intent

Build age-appropriate AI literacy through explicit vocabulary, modelling, guided practice, independent task and RAG reflection.

Key vocabulary

Input · output · data · model · prompt · evidence · bias · privacy · oversight · improvement.

Likely misconception

AI understands like a person.

Lesson sequence

  1. Retrieval starter.
  2. Teacher model with worked example.
  3. Guided pair task.
  4. Independent application.
  5. Exit check and RAG next step.

Support and stretch

Support: vocabulary cards, sentence stems, visual prompts and paired talk. Stretch: compare two decisions, identify trade-offs and defend the stronger choice.

Evidence to collect

Annotated task, prompt iteration, design sketch, audit note, RAG response or project extract.

Detailed delivery notes

Use the same lesson route in every pack so pupils experience a consistent, non-linear hub: open a topic, inspect the image, use the resources, complete the judgement task, self-assess, then export or discuss evidence. The teacher pack should remain visible beside the topic pack, not disconnected from it.

Quality assurance prompts

  • Does the student name the AI concept precisely?
  • Is there evidence, not just opinion?
  • Is the limitation specific?
  • Is the safeguard realistic and age-appropriate?
  • Is there a clear RAG next step?

🧠 Strand 1
FS2AI Conceptual Understanding

Cause, Effect and Simple Sensors

How intelligent systems learn, operate and produce outputs.

Resource links

🔗 Lesson PPT deck🔗 AI4K12 resource directory🔗 AI4K12 Five Big Ideas🔗 Google AI literacy resources

Immersive activity

Use the visual scene as the enquiry hook. Pupils take one role: designer, user, evidence checker or safety lead. Each role must ask one question, test one idea and make one improvement before the group decides whether the AI system is ready, needs revision or should not be used yet.

  • Bronze: identify what the system does.
  • Silver: explain what data, rule or instruction might affect the output.
  • Gold: judge one risk, one benefit and one improvement.
  • Platinum: defend the decision using evidence and a safeguard.

Big idea

Students predict how an AI-style system might respond to a new case and explain which features, patterns or examples influenced the output in Cause, Effect and Simple Sensors.

Teacher model

Think aloud: define the problem, name the data or evidence, test the response, identify one risk, then improve the prompt, rule, design or safeguard.

Common misconception

AI understands like a person.

Correction: AI systems produce outputs from data, rules, training patterns and objectives. Students should name the data, model, rule or objective behind the output.

Student task

Complete a claim → evidence → improvement response. Add one RAG judgement and one next-step target.

Quick check

  1. What made the system produce that output?
  2. What evidence would make the output trustworthy?
  3. What safeguard or improvement is needed?

Assessment

Emerging: names the idea with support.

Proficient: explains and applies it independently.

Advanced: evaluates trade-offs and transfers the idea.

Lesson sequence

  1. Retrieval starter: three key words and one misconception.
  2. Teacher model: think aloud from claim to evidence to judgement.
  3. Guided activity: paired role-card task using designer, user, evidence checker and safety lead.
  4. Independent application: annotated prompt, diagram, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement.
  5. Exit evidence: claim, evidence, improvement and RAG next step.

Support and stretch

Support: vocabulary cards, sentence stems, visual prompts and paired talk.

Stretch: compare two decisions, identify trade-offs and defend the stronger choice.

Evidence to collect

Annotated task, prompt iteration, design sketch, audit note, RAG response or project extract.

Extended lesson pack

Teaching sequence

Begin with a visual hook, then move through core vocabulary, teacher modelling, guided pair task, independent judgement and exit evidence. Keep the rhythm clear: retrieve, model, practise, apply, reflect.

  • Retrieval: three words and one misconception.
  • Model: teacher think-aloud using evidence.
  • Practice: role-card task with designer, user, evidence checker and safety lead.
  • Assessment: claim, evidence, improvement and RAG next step.
Evidence and QA

Collect an artefact that makes learning visible: annotated task, prompt iteration, decision logic, model card, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement. Students should identify a limitation and propose a safeguard.

  • Support: sentence stems, vocabulary cards, paired talk.
  • Stretch: compare decisions, identify trade-offs, defend the stronger choice.
  • Exit: one confidence judgement and one next step.

Correction: A strong solution meets success criteria, works for the intended user, handles edge cases and has safeguards.

Student task

Complete a claim → evidence → improvement response. Add one RAG judgement and one next-step target.

Quick check

  1. What made the system produce that output?
  2. What evidence would make the output trustworthy?
  3. What safeguard or improvement is needed?

Assessment

Emerging: names the idea with support.

Proficient: explains and applies it independently.

Advanced: evaluates trade-offs and transfers the idea.

Lesson sequence

  1. Retrieval starter: three key words and one misconception.
  2. Teacher model: think aloud from claim to evidence to judgement.
  3. Guided activity: paired role-card task using designer, user, evidence checker and safety lead.
  4. Independent application: annotated prompt, diagram, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement.
  5. Exit evidence: claim, evidence, improvement and RAG next step.

Support and stretch

Support: vocabulary cards, sentence stems, visual prompts and paired talk.

Stretch: compare two decisions, identify trade-offs and defend the stronger choice.

Evidence to collect

Annotated task, prompt iteration, design sketch, audit note, RAG response or project extract.

Privacy, fairness, accountability, human oversight and responsible innovation.

Resource links

🔗 Lesson PPT deck🔗 Common Sense AI literacy lessons🔗 Google AI literacy resources🔗 ADEK AI literacy age-band resources

Immersive activity

Use the visual scene as the enquiry hook. Pupils take one role: designer, user, evidence checker or safety lead. Each role must ask one question, test one idea and make one improvement before the group decides whether the AI system is ready, needs revision or should not be used yet.

  • Bronze: identify what the system does.
  • Silver: explain what data, rule or instruction might affect the output.
  • Gold: judge one risk, one benefit and one improvement.
  • Platinum: defend the decision using evidence and a safeguard.

Big idea

Students decide whether an AI use case should be approved, revised or rejected by weighing privacy, fairness, consent, accountability and benefit in Liability and Policy Drafting.

Teacher model

Think aloud: define the problem, name the data or evidence, test the response, identify one risk, then improve the prompt, rule, design or safeguard.

Common misconception

AI safety only means passwords.

Correction: Safety includes privacy, consent, fairness, age-appropriateness, accountability, human oversight and impact on others.

Student task

Complete a claim → evidence → improvement response. Add one RAG judgement and one next-step target.

Quick check

  1. What made the system produce that output?
  2. What evidence would make the output trustworthy?
  3. What safeguard or improvement is needed?

Assessment

Emerging: names the idea with support.

Proficient: explains and applies it independently.

Advanced: evaluates trade-offs and transfers the idea.

Lesson sequence

  1. Retrieval starter: three key words and one misconception.
  2. Teacher model: think aloud from claim to evidence to judgement.
  3. Guided activity: paired role-card task using designer, user, evidence checker and safety lead.
  4. Independent application: annotated prompt, diagram, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement.
  5. Exit evidence: claim, evidence, improvement and RAG next step.

Support and stretch

Support: vocabulary cards, sentence stems, visual prompts and paired talk.

Stretch: compare two decisions, identify trade-offs and defend the stronger choice.

Evidence to collect

Annotated task, prompt iteration, design sketch, audit note, RAG response or project extract.

Extended lesson pack

Teaching sequence

Begin with a visual hook, then move through core vocabulary, teacher modelling, guided pair task, independent judgement and exit evidence. Keep the rhythm clear: retrieve, model, practise, apply, reflect.

  • Retrieval: three words and one misconception.
  • Model: teacher think-aloud using evidence.
  • Practice: role-card task with designer, user, evidence checker and safety lead.
  • Assessment: claim, evidence, improvement and RAG next step.
Evidence and QA

Collect an artefact that makes learning visible: annotated task, prompt iteration, decision logic, model card, audit note, risk card, policy statement or design improvement. Students should identify a limitation and propose a safeguard.

  • Support: sentence stems, vocabulary cards, paired talk.
  • Stretch: compare decisions, identify trade-offs, defend the stronger choice.
  • Exit: one confidence judgement and one next step.
